newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Egypt's Mubarak ends visit to Libya with set of deals.
newsitem.headline: Egypt's Mubarak ends visit to Libya with set of deals.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Friday ended a visit to Libya with a package of deals including a yearly target of $1 billion for their trade exchanges and a free trade zone accord.

Libyan television, monitored in Tunis, said the two countries signed on Friday an accord stating that the value of trade must reach $1 billion a year, with an equal contribution by each side. In 1995, the trade exchanges between Tripoli and Cairo were estimated at $115 million.
The accord includes rules for the certificate of origin for goods exchanged and their exemption of customs procedures.
The two countries also initialled a free trade zone accord saying it would be the "core" of a larger Arab free trade zone.

Egypt's Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri and his Libyan counterpart Abdel Majid al-Gu'ud, who attended in the two-day talks, urged a joint cooperation committee to speed up projects for power and railways links, oil and gas, educational and cultural integration, as well as agriculture.
They also encouraged joint investments in the petrochemical sector and stressed the necessity for their businessmen to rely on the two countries' raw materials.
The long-awaited railways project would link the Egyptian border city of Salloum and the Libyan eastern coastal city of Tobruk.

Libyan energy sources said studies were underway for the construction of a pipeline that would transport 150,000 barrels per day of crude to an Egyptian refinery near the Mediterranean city of Alexandria.
Mubarak left Tobruk on Friday morning after two meetings with Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

A delegation of Egyptian businessmen met Gaddafi last month and announced that Cairo and Tripoli had set up a joint firm with a capital of $170 million to manufacture cars designed for the Arab markets.
Libya already signed last April a similar accord with Morocco for a car plant.
The Egyptian businessmen also announced they had set up a joint company with a $200 million capital which would invest in tourism.
They also said they would invest some $150 million to expand the Libyan iron and steel complex of Misurata to raise its production.
